vignette:
At sixty-six, she works the fitting-room counter at a department store in a suburban mall, folding and re-folding the same pile of mismatched blouses. Her hands move quickly, mechanically, but her eyes dart toward the curtains. Every time a woman pulls the curtain closed, she feels a pinch in her chest. It has been forty-four years, but the sound of a zipper still stops her breath.

She was twenty-two when it happened, newly married, newly arrived from a village in Punjab. Her husband worked long hours at a factory, and she stayed home in a small apartment, learning English from the television. One afternoon, a man from the landlord’s office came to check the gas line. He was kind, she remembers, polite and smiling. She let him in. He locked the door behind him. After that, the details come in fragments—a hand over her mouth, the weight of his body, the way she stared at a crack in the ceiling until it was over. She did not scream. She did not tell anyone. When her husband came home, she told him the gas man had fixed the stove. She never said another word.

For years she thought she had buried it. She raised two children, worked part-time at a sari shop, cooked and cleaned and prayed. But the memory did not stay buried; it simply grew roots. After her husband died of a heart attack ten years ago, the roots began to surface. She stopped sleeping. She started checking locks three, four, five times before bed. She stopped taking the bus if a man sat too close.

Now, at retail, she notices everything. The way a customer’s voice drops when asking for a smaller size. The way a man’s shadow falls across the floor. She avoids the men’s section entirely, sending her younger coworker to help male customers. When a male shopper accidentally brushes her arm reaching for a hanger, she freezes, then smiles stiffly and excuses herself to the stockroom. There she presses her back against the cold metal shelf, counting her breaths until the trembling stops.

Last week, a tall man with a deep voice asked to try on a jacket. She handed him the coat hanger without meeting his eyes. He pulled the fitting-room curtain closed, and the sound—the harsh scrape of metal rings on a rod—sent her spinning backward. She heard the crack in the ceiling again, saw the pattern of water stains, felt the hand. Her manager found her kneeling behind the counter, gripping the handle of a pair of scissors she’d grabbed from the supply drawer. She told her manager she had felt faint. She went home early that day and did not call in the next morning.

She stopped going to temple because the men there sit too close, their shoulders brushing hers. She stopped talking to her sister in India, because her sister asks too many questions about why she sounds tired. She tells herself she is fine, that the past is past, that old women do not complain about things that happened half a lifetime ago. But her body remembers what her mouth will not say.

At night, she lies awake in her apartment, tracing the outline of the ceiling crack with her eyes. She has memorized its shape. She thinks about the scissors in the supply drawer, the weight of them in her hand, and tells herself she was only trying to steady herself. She believes this, mostly.
